category.name: Databases
category.description: SQL, schema design, indexing, transactions and how databases scale.

questions.text: A single order_lines table repeats customer_name on every line. Renaming Alice on one order leaves two different names for customer 1. Which problem is this?
options: Insertion anomaly
Update anomaly
Deletion anomaly
Phantom read
questions.explanation: The same fact is stored in several rows, and an update reached only some of them, breaking customer_id → customer_name. Normalization stores the name once with its owner.

questions.text: An orders table stores products = '10,20,30' in one column. Which redesign follows first normal form?
options: Store the list as a JSON array instead of text
Add an order-items table with one row per product line
Add product_1, product_2 and product_3 columns
Move the list into a separate products_text table
questions.explanation: 1NF represents separate facts separately, so each product reference, with its quantity, gets its own row. Numbered columns still hard-code a repeating group.

questions.text: Does a DATE column violate first normal form because a date contains a year, month and day?
options: Yes, it must be split into three columns
No, it is used as one value in the model
Yes, unless it is stored as text
No, because dates are exempt from normalization
questions.explanation: "Atomic" means atomic for the chosen model, not impossible to subdivide. The 1NF concern is bundling several independently used facts into one value.

questions.text: What does the functional dependency product_id → product_title assert?
options: Equal titles imply equal product IDs
Equal product IDs imply equal titles
Product IDs are derived from the titles
A product can have several titles
questions.explanation: X → Y means knowing X determines Y. The reverse need not hold: several products can share a title.

questions.text: order_items has key (order_id, line_number) and also stores customer_id, which depends only on order_id. What is the lowest normal form this table fails?
options: First normal form
Second normal form
Fourth normal form
Fifth normal form
questions.explanation: A non-key fact depending on a proper subset of a candidate key is a partial dependency, which 2NF forbids. Move order-level facts into orders.

questions.text: orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_name) follows order_id → customer_id → customer_name. What does third normal form suggest?
options: Add customer_name to the primary key
Move customer_name to a customers table
Duplicate customer_name into order_items
Replace customer_id with customer_name
questions.explanation: The name depends on the order only through the customer, a transitive dependency. Storing it with the customer means a rename changes one row; a join reconstructs it for reports.

questions.text: A product's current price is 18.00, but an order line from last year stored 15.00. What should the design do?
options: Drop the line price and join to the current price
Keep both, because they are different facts
Update the old line to 18.00 for consistency
Store only the price that is higher
questions.explanation: The current catalog price and the price charged on a past sale describe different times. Replacing the line price with a join would destroy historical information, so it is not redundant duplication.

questions.text: customer_id alone uniquely identifies a customer row. What is (customer_id, email)?
options: A candidate key
A non-minimal superkey
A composite foreign key
A partial dependency
questions.explanation: It identifies rows, so it is a superkey, but it is not minimal: removing email still leaves an identifier. A candidate key is a minimal identifier.

questions.text: In enrolment(student, subject, teacher), each teacher teaches exactly one subject, so teacher → subject, but a teacher has many students. What is the lowest normal form this relation fails?
options: Second normal form (2NF)
Third normal form (3NF)
Boyce–Codd normal form
First normal form (1NF)
questions.explanation: Every attribute belongs to a candidate key, so 3NF's prime-attribute exception is met. BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey, and teacher is not.

questions.text: The enrolment relation is split into (teacher, subject) and (student, teacher). What is the main cost of this BCNF decomposition?
options: The join can invent false teacher–subject pairs
One-teacher-per-subject needs a cross-table rule
Each student's name must now be stored twice
The split loses each student's teacher assignment
questions.explanation: The split is lossless, but the simple keys no longer stop Alice having two Databases teachers. This is why dependency preservation matters alongside losslessness.

questions.text: A customer's preferred languages and favourite categories are independent lists stored together as (customer, language, category). Which design follows fourth normal form?
options: Keep one table but make category nullable
Store languages and categories in two separate tables
Concatenate languages into one column per customer
Add a surrogate key to the combined table
questions.explanation: Independent multivalued facts force a row for every language/category pairing. Separating them removes those repeated combinations. If the lists were not independent, the split would invent preferences.

questions.text: Approved triples are (S1, P1, J1), (S1, P2, J2) and (S2, P1, J2). If you store only the three pairwise projections and join them back, which unapproved triple appears?
options: (S2, P2, J1)
(S1, P1, J2)
(S2, P1, J1)
(S1, P2, J1)
questions.explanation: The pairs (S1, P1), (S1, J2) and (P1, J2) all exist, so the join creates a spurious tuple. 5NF analysis checks whether a multiway relationship really decomposes.

questions.text: What makes a decomposition lossless?
options: Every table keeps the original primary key
Rejoining yields exactly the original facts
No column appears in more than one piece
Every piece has the same number of rows
questions.explanation: A lossless split loses no facts and adds no false combinations when rejoined. Splitting names and emails into tables with no reliable link would fail this test.

questions.text: A sample table shows every book with exactly one author. What can you conclude about the dependency book_id → author_id?
options: It holds, because the sample has no counterexample
Nothing yet: dependencies come from business rules
It holds only after you add a unique index
It never holds for many-to-many data
questions.explanation: A sample without contradictions does not prove a rule. Ask the business whether co-authored books are forbidden before designing around it.

questions.text: To speed up order pages, you add a stored total_cents column to orders. What new responsibility does this create?
options: Every read must recompute the total to verify it
Every write to order lines must also update the total
The order_items table can now be dropped
The total must be indexed to be correct
questions.explanation: A stored aggregate is a second representation of a calculation. Every path that changes line items must maintain it, or a drift-detection and rebuild process must exist.

questions.text: A denormalized summary is maintained by a periodic background job instead of in the writing transaction. What must readers accept?
options: Writes to the source table are blocked during refresh
They may see values older than the source data
The summary can never drift from the source
The source table must become read-only
questions.explanation: Background refresh trades freshness for cheaper writes. Record refresh progress and agree on how much staleness is acceptable.

questions.text: A report joining orders and lines is slow. What do the notes recommend before adding a denormalized copy?
options: Convert the whole schema to a document store
Inspect the plan, indexes and rows actually read
Duplicate the line columns into orders
Add an application cache in front of every query
questions.explanation: A suitable index or a smaller result can remove the bottleneck without duplicating data. Denormalization should be justified by measurement and documented with its authoritative source.

questions.text:
With SQLite foreign keys enabled, what happens to staff rows when their department is deleted?

CREATE TABLE staff (
    staff_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    department_id INTEGER REFERENCES departments(department_id)
        ON DELETE SET NULL,
    name TEXT NOT NULL
);
options: They are deleted along with the department
They stay, with department_id set to NULL
The department delete is rejected with an error
They keep the old ID, which now dangles
questions.explanation: SET NULL retains the employee but removes the reference, which requires the column to be nullable. CASCADE would delete the staff rows; RESTRICT would reject the delete.

questions.text: Why might ON DELETE CASCADE from customers to orders be the wrong choice?
options: Cascades are not supported on foreign keys
It could erase order history needed for accounting
It makes every customer insert much slower
It prevents any customer from ever being deleted
questions.explanation: Cascade should be chosen because dependent rows are meant to disappear, not to silence a foreign-key error. Historical orders often need retention or anonymization instead.

questions.text: In SQLite, a child row's foreign key is declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. Inside one transaction you insert the child, then its parent, then commit. What happens?
options: The child insert fails immediately
The commit succeeds because the reference is valid at commit
The commit succeeds even if the parent is never inserted
SQLite ignores the deferral and rejects the commit
questions.explanation: Deferral moves the check to commit time. Without the parent insert, the commit itself would fail.

questions.text: A cinema has UNIQUE (screening_id, seat_number). Which booking is rejected after (100, 'A1') is stored?
questions.explanation: The pair must be unique, not each column on its own. Seat A1 can be booked for other screenings.

questions.text: An application checks "is this seat free?" and then inserts a booking. Why does the notes' design still rely on a unique constraint?
options: Constraints always run faster than any SELECT
Two clients can both pass the check before either inserts
The check cannot read uncommitted rows of its own
Unique constraints also lock the whole bookings table
questions.explanation: A check followed by a write races with concurrent writers. The database rule is evaluated for every insert, so only one booking for the pair can succeed.

questions.text: Which kind of integrity does CHECK (price_cents >= 0) protect?
options: Entity integrity
Referential integrity
Domain integrity
Business integrity
questions.explanation: Domain integrity limits an attribute's allowed values. Entity integrity concerns unambiguous identifiers, referential integrity valid relationships, and business integrity larger multi-row invariants.

questions.text: In an ordinary (non-STRICT) SQLite table, what happens when you insert 'abc' into an INTEGER column?
options: It is rejected with a datatype mismatch
It is stored as text due to type affinity
It is silently converted to the integer 0
It is stored as NULL instead
questions.explanation: Ordinary SQLite tables use type affinity rather than strict enforcement. A STRICT table (SQLite 3.37+) rejects the value; PostgreSQL also rejects it.

questions.text: In the conceptual, logical and physical design levels, which one does "index orders.customer_id" belong to?
options: Conceptual
Logical
Physical
Requirements
questions.explanation: An index is an access-path decision for a particular engine. "An order has a customer" is conceptual, and "store customer_id as a foreign key" is logical.

questions.text: A customer_preferences table uses customer_id as both its primary key and a foreign key to customers. What relationship does this implement?
options: One-to-many
One-to-zero-or-one
Many-to-many
Exactly one-to-one
questions.explanation: The primary key prevents a second preference row for a customer, and the foreign key requires the customer to exist. Nothing forces every customer to have a preference row.

questions.text: Orders can contain many products, and products appear in many orders. How is this represented relationally?
options: A product_ids array column on orders
A junction table like order_items
A foreign key from products to orders
A self-join on the orders table
questions.explanation: A junction table records each order–product association as its own row, here with quantity and purchase price. Its composite key (order_id, line_number) identifies each line.

questions.text: Which rule can a foreign key from order_items to orders not enforce on its own?
options: Each item refers to an existing order
Every completed order has at least one item
An item cannot point to a missing order ID
Deleting an order affects its items
questions.explanation: A foreign key checks that referenced rows exist. "At least one item" involves several rows and the checkout workflow, so it needs a deliberate implementation.

questions.text: Which performance requirement is testable enough to guide design?
options: "Order history pages should always feel fast to customers."
"95% of order-history requests finish in 200 ms at 500 req/s."
"The database should scale well as the business grows."
"Queries should use indexes wherever that is possible."
questions.explanation: A useful target names the latency, the proportion of requests and the expected traffic. "Fast" or "scales well" cannot be evaluated or tested.

questions.text: How do sharding and replication differ?
options: Sharding copies all data to every node; replication splits it
Sharding splits data across nodes; replication keeps copies of it
Sharding applies only to NoSQL; replication only to SQL
They are two names for the same technique
questions.explanation: Sharding places different subsets of data on different nodes, while replication keeps the same data on several nodes. They are orthogonal and are often combined.

questions.text: What distinguishes sharding from table partitioning on a single server?
options: Partitions cannot be defined by a hash function
Shards live on separate servers across a network
Partitioning always needs distributed transactions
Sharded tables are not allowed to have indexes
questions.explanation: Partitioning divides a table within one database instance. Sharding distributes those pieces across machines, adding routing, cross-shard queries and resharding as new problems.

questions.text: Orders are range-sharded by created_at. What happens to new inserts?
options: They spread evenly across all of the shards
They all land on the shard holding the newest range
They are rejected until a new shard is created
They are copied to every shard
questions.explanation: A monotonically increasing range key sends every new row to the latest range, creating a write hotspot. Hashing spreads writes but makes range scans span shards.

questions.text: Users and their orders and sessions are sharded by user_id. Which query must be sent to every shard?
options: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE product_id = 7;
UPDATE users SET name = 'A' WHERE user_id = 42;
DELETE FROM sessions WHERE user_id = 42;
questions.explanation: A query without the shard key cannot be routed to one shard, so it becomes a scatter-gather across all of them. Choose the shard key from the most important access patterns.

questions.text: With simple modulo hashing (hash(key) % N), adding one server remaps most keys. What does consistent hashing change?
options: No keys ever move when nodes change
Only keys in the new node's arc of the ring move
Every key moves exactly once to the new node
Keys are reassigned randomly across all nodes
questions.explanation: On a hash ring, a new node takes over only part of one neighbour's interval. Keys elsewhere on the ring keep their assignments.

questions.text: What do virtual nodes add to consistent hashing?
options: They make a single hot key spread across many servers
Each server gets many ring points, smoothing load
They remove the need for replication
They guarantee no key ever moves
questions.explanation: Many points per physical server even out arc sizes and let bigger servers take proportionally more. A single hot key still lands on one owner.

questions.text: What does "consistency" mean in the CAP theorem?
options: Every transaction preserves the database's constraints
Operations behave as if on one up-to-date copy (linearizability)
All replicas store their data in the same on-disk format
Every write eventually becomes visible to all readers
questions.explanation: CAP consistency is a linearizability-style guarantee about reads and writes. It is unrelated to ACID consistency, which means preserving declared rules and invariants.

questions.text: Three replicas are split into A | B–C by a network partition. A consistency-first system uses majority quorums. What happens on A's side?
options: A keeps accepting authoritative writes
A refuses or delays operations that need a quorum
A becomes the new primary because it is isolated
A merges its writes with B and C later
questions.explanation: A alone cannot form a majority of two, so it must fail or wait for strongly consistent operations. That is exactly the consistency-over-availability choice CAP predicts; quorums implement the trade-off rather than beat it.

questions.text: A Cassandra table has replication factor 3, and both reads and writes use QUORUM. Why does a read meet the latest acknowledged write under the documented model?
options: QUORUM waits for all three replicas
R + W = 4 > 3, so the read and write sets overlap
QUORUM always reads from the coordinator node
Writes at QUORUM are applied synchronously everywhere
questions.explanation: A quorum of 3 is 2. Any two replicas read and any two written must share at least one node. With ONE for both, R + W = 2 and a read can miss the write.

questions.text: Why is a single PostgreSQL server not a counterexample to CAP?
options: Its MVCC snapshots remove network partitions
It has no replicas; if it fails, it is unavailable
It gives up consistency in order to stay available
It runs consensus internally between its processes
questions.explanation: CAP concerns replicated copies during a network partition. A lone server is simply a different failure model: if it is unreachable, availability disappears.

questions.text: Two replicas accept concurrent updates to the same cart during a partition. After reconnecting, they resolve with last-write-wins. What is the risk?
options: The replicas can never converge again
One acknowledged update is silently discarded
Both updates are applied twice
Reads block until an operator picks a winner
questions.explanation: Last-write-wins converges by keeping the update with the later timestamp, which can drop the other change. Convergence and preserving every update are different properties.

questions.text: What do vector clocks let a replicated store detect?
options: The physical time of every write
That two versions were written concurrently
Which replica has the most free disk space
Whether a network partition has ended yet
questions.explanation: Vector clocks track causal history, distinguishing "one version supersedes the other" from "neither saw the other". Concurrent versions then need an application or CRDT-style merge.

questions.text: Under eventual consistency, what is guaranteed?
options: Every read returns the latest write
If updates stop, replicas converge to the same value
Writes are rejected during a partition
Replicas agree within a fixed number of milliseconds
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency promises convergence, not freshness at any moment or a time bound. Applications must tolerate stale reads in between.

questions.text: A user updates their profile on the primary and the next page reads from an asynchronous replica. What can happen?
options: The write is rolled back on the primary
The page shows the old profile because of replication lag
The replica rejects the read until it has fully caught up
The replica forwards the write back to the primary
questions.explanation: Asynchronous replicas apply changes after the primary commits, so an immediate read may be stale. Read-your-writes needs routing that user's reads to the primary or waiting for the replica to reach the write's position.

questions.text: With asynchronous replication, the primary crashes and a replica is promoted. What can be lost?
options: Nothing, because every commit waits for the replica
Acknowledged commits not yet sent to the replica
Only uncommitted transactions running on the replica
Every transaction since the last full backup
questions.explanation: The primary acknowledges before replicas confirm, leaving a data-loss window. Synchronous replication narrows it at the cost of commit latency.

questions.text: With a synchronous standby configured, which PostgreSQL synchronous_commit level waits until the standby has replayed the change so it is visible to standby queries?
options: local
remote_write
on
remote_apply
questions.explanation: on waits for a durable WAL flush on the standby, which is not the same as replay. remote_apply waits for replay, giving read visibility on that standby.

questions.text: What is a cost of synchronous replication to a standby in another region?
options: Replicas can no longer be promoted
Each commit waits for a network round trip to the standby
The primary stops writing WAL locally
It allows more committed data to be lost on failover
questions.explanation: Commit latency includes the round trip, and an unavailable synchronous standby can stall commits. Durability improves while latency and availability dependencies grow.

questions.text: After a network split, an old primary and a newly promoted replica both accept writes. What is this called and what prevents it?
options: Replication lag; a larger WAL buffer
Split brain; fencing the old primary
Write skew; Serializable isolation
Read repair; anti-entropy
questions.explanation: Two nodes acting as primary create divergent histories. Fencing excludes the old primary, through storage, network or power controls, before the new one takes writes.

questions.text: A standby with a PostgreSQL physical replication slot goes offline for 10 hours. What risk does the primary face?
options: The slot silently drops and the standby resyncs automatically
Retained WAL accumulates and can fill the primary's disk
The primary stops accepting writes immediately
The slot replays WAL to the primary itself
questions.explanation: A slot keeps WAL until its consumer receives it. Monitor slot lag and consider max_slot_wal_keep_size to cap retention.

questions.text: You need to replicate only two tables into a database running a newer PostgreSQL major version. Which kind of replication fits?
options: Physical WAL streaming replication to a standby
Logical replication (publications/subscriptions)
A block-level copy of the data directory
Synchronous physical streaming replication
questions.explanation: Logical replication sends row changes and can select tables and cross versions. Physical replication copies storage-level changes for a whole cluster and is tightly coupled to the engine version.

questions.text: What can happen to MySQL semisynchronous replication when no replica acknowledges within the timeout?
options: The source rolls back every pending transaction
It can fall back to asynchronous replication
The source shuts down to protect the data
It promotes the slowest replica automatically
questions.explanation: After the timeout, the source can continue without acknowledgement, so the durability guarantee quietly weakens until a replica catches up. Monitor for this state.

questions.text: In a Galera cluster, two nodes update the same row concurrently. What typically happens at commit?
options: Both commits succeed and the values are merged
The later-certified transaction fails and must be retried
The node with the higher ID always wins
Both transactions are blocked until an operator intervenes
questions.explanation: Galera executes locally and certifies write sets in a global order. A conflicting later write set is aborted, so applications need retry logic, especially around hot rows.

questions.text: Why are AUTO_INCREMENT values not contiguous in a multi-primary Galera cluster?
options: Galera reuses freed IDs after rows are deleted
Nodes use interleaved offsets to avoid collisions
IDs are generated from node timestamps instead
Galera disables AUTO_INCREMENT on all tables
questions.explanation: Automatic increment control adjusts the increment and offset by cluster size, so three nodes might generate 1, 4, 7 and 2, 5, 8. Gaps are expected.

questions.text: A Cassandra table is declared PRIMARY KEY ((customer_id), event_time, event_id). Which query fits it?
options: All events of a given type across every customer
One customer's events within a time range
All events in a time range across every customer
Customers ordered by their total number of events
questions.explanation: customer_id is the partition key, and the clustering columns order rows inside each partition. Queries should target one partition and read a range of clustering keys.

questions.text: A Cassandra partition keyed only by sensor_id grows without bound as readings accumulate. What is the usual fix?
options: Add ALLOW FILTERING to the read queries
Partition by (sensor_id, day) instead
Create a secondary index on sensor_id
Lower the replication factor to 1
questions.explanation: Bucketing bounds each partition's size while keeping a sensor's recent data together. ALLOW FILTERING permits unsupported queries but does not fix the model.

questions.text: Why does Cassandra write a tombstone when data is deleted instead of erasing it immediately?
options: To let users undo deletes for a fixed period
So an offline replica cannot resurrect the data
Because SSTable files can never be modified
To keep deleted data visible to later reads
questions.explanation: A deletion marker lets replicas that missed the delete learn about it during repair. Large numbers of tombstones can slow reads until compaction removes them.

questions.text: A MongoDB customer document stores every login event in one ever-growing array. What do the notes recommend?
options: Keep the array and raise the document size limit
Store events as separate documents or bounded buckets
Move the array into a nested object
Index the array to keep writes cheap
questions.explanation: Unbounded arrays cause document growth, expensive rewrites, large payloads and size-limit problems. Separate event documents or month buckets give each document a planned upper size.

questions.text: An order always shows its few shipping addresses, which are read together and rarely change. Which document design fits?
options: Embed the addresses in the order document
Store each address in a separate collection by reference
Store addresses in a key-value cache only
Duplicate the addresses into every product document
questions.explanation: One-to-few, bounded data read with its parent suits embedding and loads in one read. References suit large, unbounded or widely shared data.

questions.text: Inventory must keep available and reserved consistent. Why do the notes suggest storing both in one MongoDB document?
options: Documents cannot hold more than one counter
Updates to a single document are atomic
It removes the need for any index
Separate documents cannot be updated at all
questions.explanation: Document databases commonly guarantee atomicity per document, so the document boundary is a correctness decision. Updating several documents together needs multi-document transactions where the engine supports them.

questions.text: In MongoDB, which documents does the filter {nickname: null} match?
options: Only documents where nickname is explicitly null
Documents where nickname is null or missing
Only documents without a nickname field
No documents, because null never compares equal
questions.explanation: The null filter is broader than many expect. Add $exists: true for explicit nulls only, or use $exists: false for missing fields only.

questions.text: A client calls MongoDB replaceOne with only {name: "Ana"} for a user document that also had email. What happens to email?
options: It is kept unchanged alongside the new name
It is removed, since the whole body is replaced
It is kept, but its value becomes null
The call fails because email is missing
questions.explanation: Replacement writes a new document body except _id. A partial update with updateOne and $set changes only the named fields.

questions.text: A popular Redis cache key expires and thousands of requests miss at once, all querying the database. Which mitigation targets this?
options: Removing the TTL from every cached key
Single-flight rebuilds with jittered TTLs
Storing the value in a larger Redis hash
Switching the cache to write-behind mode
questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede. Letting one request rebuild the value while others wait, and spreading expiry times with jitter, prevents a burst of identical database queries.

questions.text: In a Neo4j graph, a Country {name: "US"} node connects to hundreds of millions of users. Why is traversing through it a problem?
options: Nodes cannot have more than one label
It is a supernode, so traversals fan out enormously
Relationships pointing to it cannot carry properties
Cypher cannot match nodes by a property
questions.explanation: A very high-degree node makes any path through it expensive. Alternatives include filtering by property, partitioning relationships or avoiding traversal through global hubs.

questions.text: Code writes an order to PostgreSQL and then indexes it in a search engine. The second write fails. What pattern do the notes recommend?
options: Swap the order: write the search index first
Record the change in an outbox or CDC stream and project it
Retry the search write forever inside the web request
Wrap both writes in a database savepoint
questions.explanation: This is the dual-write problem; reversing the order only reverses the failure. Deriving the search index from a durable change log, plus reconciliation, keeps one source of truth.

questions.text: A B-tree index exists on orders(customer_id, status, order_date). Which filter can it serve least directly with a normal index seek?
options: WHERE customer_id = 42
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'open'
WHERE status = 'open'
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'open' AND order_date >= '2026-10-01'
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree is ordered by its leading column first. Without a customer_id condition, open rows are spread across every customer group, so there is no single prefix to seek to.

questions.text:
Which index best supports this query?

SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date >= '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY order_date;
options: (customer_id, order_date)
(order_date, customer_id)
(order_date) alone
(order_id, customer_id)
questions.explanation: Equality on the leading column puts all of customer 42's entries together, and the second column then gives the range and the sort order. Leading with the date would interleave every customer in the range.

questions.text: A query filters tenant_id = ?, status = ? and created_at >= ?, and orders by created_at. Which column order is the natural starting candidate?
options: (created_at, tenant_id, status)
(tenant_id, status, created_at)
(status, created_at, tenant_id)
(created_at, status, tenant_id)
questions.explanation: Equality columns form the prefix, and the range column comes last so the engine can walk it in order. This is a heuristic to verify with plans, not a universal formula.

questions.text:
What does INCLUDE (total_cents) change in this PostgreSQL index?

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date
ON orders(customer_id, order_date DESC)
INCLUDE (total_cents);
options: total_cents becomes a third sort key
total_cents is stored as payload for covering reads
The index now enforces uniqueness on total_cents
Rows with a null total_cents are excluded
questions.explanation: Included columns are non-key payload, so they affect neither search order nor uniqueness. They let a query that also returns total_cents be answered from the index.

questions.text: A PostgreSQL index covers every column a query needs, yet the plan still shows heap fetches. Why?
options: Covering indexes are ignored when sorting
Pages not marked all-visible need heap checks
PostgreSQL always reads the heap for every row
The index was built without CONCURRENTLY
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL indexes do not store full row-visibility state. The visibility map lets an index-only scan skip the heap only for all-visible pages, so frequently updated tables benefit less.

questions.text: Which query can use the partial index ON orders(customer_id, order_date DESC) WHERE status = 'open'?
options: WHERE customer_id = 42
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'open'
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'closed'
WHERE status IN ('open', 'closed')
questions.explanation: The index contains only open orders, so the planner must prove the query's condition implies status = 'open'. A query for all or closed orders needs rows the index omits.

questions.text: created_at has a B-tree index. Which predicate selects October 1, 2026 in a form that can use a normal range scan?
options: WHERE DATE(created_at) = DATE '2026-10-01'
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-02'
WHERE CAST(created_at AS TEXT) LIKE '2026-10-01%'
WHERE EXTRACT(DAY FROM created_at) = 1 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM created_at) = 10
questions.explanation: Wrapping the indexed column in a function hides its ordering unless a matching expression index exists. A half-open range on the raw column stays sargable.

questions.text: Logins look up users with WHERE lower(email) = lower($1). Which index matches that predicate?
options: CREATE INDEX ON users (email);
CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email));
CREATE INDEX ON users USING hash (email);
CREATE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
questions.explanation: An expression index stores the computed value, so the planner can match an identical expression in the query. A plain index on email orders the raw values, not their lowercase forms.

questions.text: Which predicate is a PostgreSQL hash index unable to accelerate?
options: session_token = $1
created_at BETWEEN $1 AND $2
api_key = 'abc-123-xyz-456'
email = 'a@example.com'
questions.explanation: Hashing maps keys to buckets and does not preserve order, so it suits equality only. A B-tree handles both equality and ranges and is usually the more versatile choice.

questions.text: A huge append-only events table is written in time order, and queries scan narrow time windows. Which PostgreSQL index type can be much smaller than a B-tree here?
options: GIN
Hash
BRIN
GiST
questions.explanation: BRIN summarizes ranges of table pages, which works well when the value correlates with physical row order. GIN suits containment and full-text search; hash suits equality.

questions.text: Which PostgreSQL index type fits WHERE tags @> ARRAY['postgres'] on an array column?
options: BRIN
GIN
Hash
A B-tree on tags
questions.explanation: GIN is an inverted index that maps elements to the rows containing them, which fits array and document containment. Ordering-based B-trees cannot answer "contains this element" directly.

questions.text: Why does a B-tree on body not help WHERE body LIKE '%database%'?
options: B-trees cannot store text columns
A leading wildcard gives no prefix to seek to
LIKE is always executed as a full sort
The pattern is case-insensitive by default
questions.explanation: B-tree ordering helps only when the beginning of the value is known. Use full-text search, a trigram index such as pg_trgm, or a search engine for substring and word queries.

questions.text: In MySQL InnoDB, why does a wide primary key such as a long string make secondary indexes larger?
options: InnoDB copies the whole row into each secondary index
Each secondary index entry stores the primary-key value
Secondary indexes must include every key column twice
Wide keys disable index compression
questions.explanation: InnoDB clusters rows by primary key, and secondary entries locate rows by carrying that key value rather than a heap address. PostgreSQL secondary indexes instead point to heap tuples.

questions.text: You run PostgreSQL CLUSTER orders USING idx_orders_date;. What happens to rows inserted afterwards?
options: They are always placed in index order
They are not kept in that order automatically
They are rejected until CLUSTER runs again
They are routed to a separate clustered table
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's CLUSTER is a one-time physical reorder of a heap table. In SQL Server and InnoDB, "clustered" instead means a persistent storage organization that is maintained.

questions.text: 98% of rows have status = 'active'. The plan for WHERE status = 'active' uses a sequential scan. What is the most likely reading?
options: The index is corrupt and needs REINDEX
Scanning beats random lookups for most rows
The optimizer ignores indexes on text columns
Statistics must be stale since a scan was chosen
questions.explanation: A predicate that matches most rows is not selective. Visiting nearly every row through an index adds random I/O, so a scan is often the correct plan.

questions.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows an estimate of 10 rows but an actual count of 2,000,000 after a large backfill. What should you check first?
options: Whether the connection pool is large enough
Whether statistics are stale (run ANALYZE)
Whether the query selects every column
Whether fsync is enabled on the server
questions.explanation: Row estimates come from statistics, and a bulk change can leave them describing the old table. Bad estimates drive poor join orders and access paths.

questions.text: The optimizer badly underestimates WHERE country = 'DE' AND currency = 'EUR'. What is the likely cause?
options: The two columns lack a combined index
It treats correlated predicates as independent
Text comparisons are always estimated at one row
The query is missing a LIMIT clause
questions.explanation: Multiplying separate selectivities underestimates strongly related columns. Some engines, including PostgreSQL, support extended multicolumn statistics for such cases.

questions.text: When is a nested loop join a good plan?
options: When both inputs are huge and unsorted
When the outer input is small and the inner lookup is indexed
When the join condition is a range on unindexed columns
When memory is too small for any sort
questions.explanation: A nested loop does one inner lookup per outer row, which is cheap for few outer rows with an indexed inner side. It degrades badly when the outer input is unexpectedly large.

questions.text: Which join algorithm builds an in-memory table from one input and probes it with the other, and is common for equality joins?
options: Nested loop join
Merge join
Hash join
Cross join
questions.explanation: A hash join hashes one side and looks up each row of the other side. Memory pressure can make it spill to disk; a merge join instead relies on sorted inputs.

questions.text: An API serves ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000. Why do deep pages get slower?
options: OFFSET disables all indexes
The engine still reads and discards the skipped rows
Each page reopens a new connection
LIMIT forces a full table sort on every single call
questions.explanation: Offset pagination must walk past every earlier row. Keyset pagination resumes from the last row's (created_at, id) and, with a matching index, avoids that prefix.

questions.text: Which condition fetches the next keyset page after the row (created_at = $2, id = $3) for ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC?
options: WHERE created_at < $2 AND id < $3
WHERE created_at < $2 OR (created_at = $2 AND id < $3)
WHERE created_at <= $2 AND id <> $3
WHERE created_at <= $2 AND (id <= $3 OR id IS NULL)
questions.explanation: The cursor must follow the full ordering: older timestamps, or the same timestamp with a smaller ID. Separate AND conditions skip, repeat or re-include rows; in PostgreSQL (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) is equivalent.

questions.text: A page loads 100 customers, then runs one orders query per customer in a loop. How many queries does the request issue?
questions.explanation: This is the N+1 pattern: one list query plus one per row. Each statement may be fast, but round trips add up; fix it with a join, one IN query or eager loading.

questions.text: Ten application instances each use a connection pool of 50. What should you check before raising the pool size to "speed things up"?
options: That each pool uses a different database user
That the database can serve 500 connections
That every query uses a prepared statement
That autocommit is disabled in every instance
questions.explanation: Fleet-wide connections multiply: 10 × 50 = 500. Larger pools can add memory use, lock contention and tail latency, so size them from measured database capacity.

questions.text: With cache-aside, a writer commits a new price and deletes the cache key. How can the cache still end up stale?
options: Deleting a key always fails under heavy load
A slow reader can re-cache the old value
Cache-aside never reads from the database
The cache refuses keys deleted within the TTL
questions.explanation: A reader may load the old database value, the writer then commits and invalidates, and the reader finally stores its old value. Versioned values, ordered events or short TTLs reduce this race.

questions.text: What is the main risk of a write-behind cache compared with caching read-only copies?
options: Reads always bypass the cache and hit the database
Acknowledged writes may be lost before persisting
It cannot store values that have a TTL
It requires one materialized view per cached key
questions.explanation: Write-behind accepts a write and persists it later, so a crash can lose, reorder or duplicate acknowledged changes. Two systems do not become one atomic transaction because of a strategy name.

questions.text: What does PostgreSQL require before REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY can run?
options: The view must have been created WITH NO DATA
A suitable unique index on the materialized view
An exclusive lock on every base table
A trigger on each source table
questions.explanation: The concurrent refresh compares old and new results by a unique key so readers can keep querying during the refresh. A plain refresh blocks readers of the view instead.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, what does an UPDATE to a row generally do physically?
options: Overwrites the existing row in place on its page
Writes a new row version and leaves the old one dead
Deletes the row and renumbers the whole table
Writes the change only to the WAL, not the table
questions.explanation: Under MVCC, an update creates a new tuple version. Old versions remain until no transaction needs them, and vacuum then makes their space reusable.

questions.text: A PostgreSQL table had millions of rows deleted and then vacuumed, but its file is about the same size. What does this usually mean?
options: Vacuum failed and must be rerun with FULL
The freed space is reusable inside the table
The deleted rows are still visible to queries
Autovacuum was disabled for that table
questions.explanation: Normal vacuum marks dead-tuple space as reusable without returning it to the operating system. Future writes reuse it; shrinking the file needs more disruptive rewrite operations.

questions.text: Dead tuples keep growing even though autovacuum runs regularly. Which application behaviour is a common cause?
options: Using prepared statements for every query
Sessions left idle in an open transaction
Selecting only the columns each page needs
Paginating results with keyset cursors
questions.explanation: A long-running or idle transaction holds an old snapshot, so vacuum cannot remove row versions it might still need. Fix transaction boundaries rather than only tuning vacuum harder.

questions.text: Events are range-partitioned by month and kept for 12 months. What is usually the cheapest way to remove the oldest month?
options: DELETE FROM events WHERE event_time < ...
Detach and drop that month's partition
Run VACUUM FULL on the parent table
UPDATE old rows to set deleted_at
questions.explanation: Dropping a partition removes a whole object, avoiding row-by-row deletes, dead tuples and index maintenance. Retention is a major reason to partition by time.

questions.text: A table is partitioned by event_time. Which query lets the planner prune unrelated partitions?
options: WHERE user_id = 42
WHERE event_time >= '2026-10-01' AND event_time < '2026-11-01'
WHERE event_type = 'login'
ORDER BY event_time DESC LIMIT 10 with no WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Pruning requires a predicate on the partition key. Filters on other columns must examine every partition, which is why the partition key must match the access patterns.

questions.text: A table has eight indexes. What happens to the cost of each INSERT?
options: It stays the same; indexes only affect reads
It rises, because every index must also be updated
It falls, because inserts find free pages faster
It rises only for indexes that are unique
questions.explanation: Each index is another stored structure to maintain on inserts, deletes and updates of indexed columns. Every extra index must earn its write, storage and maintenance cost.

questions.text: Why might you use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a busy PostgreSQL table?
options: It builds the index faster than a normal build
It avoids blocking writes during the build
It can run inside an explicit transaction block
It guarantees that the build cannot fail
questions.explanation: A concurrent build does more total work and takes longer, but it does not hold locks that block normal writes. It cannot run inside a transaction block and may leave an invalid index on failure.

questions.text: pg_stat_user_indexes shows zero scans for an index. Why should you not drop it immediately?
options: Zero scans means every query already uses it
It may back a unique constraint or rare jobs
Dropping an index also drops its table
Scan counts include only sequential scans
questions.explanation: Statistics can reset, and an index may back a uniqueness rule, foreign-key checks or a monthly report. Understand the observation period and purpose first.

questions.text: A report sums amount across hundreds of millions of sales. Which storage layout tends to suit it?
options: Row storage, keeping each sale together
Column storage, reading mainly amount
A wide-column store keyed by sale ID
A key-value store with one sale per key
questions.explanation: Columnar engines store each field's values together, so an aggregate reads mostly the needed column. Wide-column databases like Cassandra are a different design organized around partition keys.

questions.text:
Alice has two orders, Bob has one and Carol has none. What order_count does this query report for Carol?

SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;
options: NULL
Carol's row is not returned
questions.explanation: The left join preserves Carol as one null-extended row, and COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(o.order_id) would ignore the null order ID and report 0.

questions.text: Every customer must stay in a report, but only their open orders should be attached. Where does o.status = 'open' belong in a customers LEFT JOIN orders query?
options: In the join's ON condition
In the WHERE clause
In a HAVING clause after grouping
In the ORDER BY clause
questions.explanation: In ON it limits which orders match while unmatched customers are still kept. In WHERE it filters the joined result, removing customers whose order columns are null, so the left join behaves like an inner join.

questions.text:
The blocked table contains the values 2 and NULL. Customers have IDs 1, 2 and 3. What does this query return?

SELECT customer_id
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked);
options: IDs 1 and 3
IDs 1, 2 and 3
No rows
Only ID 2
questions.explanation: For IDs 1 and 3, comparing with the null yields unknown, so NOT IN never becomes true. A correlated NOT EXISTS expresses "no matching blocked row" and returns IDs 1 and 3.

questions.text: Which query lists customers who have never placed an order without being affected by null values in orders.customer_id?
options: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
SELECT name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id <> c.customer_id;
SELECT name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status IS NOT NULL;
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS asks whether any matching order row exists, so a null in another order cannot make the test unknown. The <> join pairs every customer with other customers' orders instead.

questions.text: Which query finds departments with at least two employees earning more than 60000?
options: SELECT dept_id FROM employees WHERE salary > 60000 GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
SELECT dept_id FROM employees WHERE COUNT(*) >= 2 AND salary > 60000 GROUP BY dept_id;
SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING salary > 60000;
SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id WHERE COUNT(*) >= 2;
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, and HAVING tests the resulting group count. Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE, and a bare non-grouped column in HAVING is invalid or meaningless.

questions.text:
No employee row matches the filter. What does this query return?

SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(salary) AS total
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id < 0;
options: No rows at all
One row: n = 0, total = NULL
One row: n = 0, total = 0
One row: n = NULL, total = NULL
questions.explanation: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row. Counts of empty input are zero, while SUM and AVG return null; with a GROUP BY key there would be no groups and no rows.

questions.text: The salary column holds 100, 200 and NULL. What does AVG(salary) return?
options: NULL
questions.explanation: Aggregates skip nulls, so the average is taken over the two known values. AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0)) would treat the unknown salary as a real zero and return 100.

questions.text: Joining employees to their projects duplicated salaries for people on several projects. Why is SUM(DISTINCT salary) not a correct fix?
options: DISTINCT cannot be combined with SUM
Two different employees with equal salaries are counted once
It still adds each duplicated salary several more times
It returns null when any salary repeats
questions.explanation: DISTINCT deduplicates numeric values, not facts. Deduplication must use the identity of what is counted; aggregate employees separately before joining the one-to-many relationship.

questions.text:
What RANK() and DENSE_RANK() values does the row with amount 200 receive?

WITH t(id, amount) AS (VALUES (1, 100), (2, 100), (3, 200))
SELECT id,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS r,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS d
FROM t;
options: r = 2, d = 2
r = 3, d = 2
r = 3, d = 3
r = 2, d = 3
questions.explanation: Both 100-valued rows tie at rank 1. RANK() leaves a gap after ties, so the next rank is 3, while DENSE_RANK() continues with 2.

questions.text:
What running total does the first row (id = 1) show?

WITH t(id, amount) AS (VALUES (1, 100), (2, 100), (3, 200))
SELECT id, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS running
FROM t
ORDER BY id;
options: NULL
questions.explanation: The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, which includes the whole peer group of tied values. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW with a unique order to advance one row at a time.

questions.text: LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) returns each row's own amount instead of the partition's final amount. What fixes it?
options: Add PARTITION BY id and keep ORDER BY id
Add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
Replace it with LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id)
Sort both the window and outer query with ORDER BY id DESC
questions.explanation: The default ordered frame ends at the current row's peers, so the "last" value in that frame is the current one. Extending the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING lets it see the end of the partition.

questions.text: You need the top two sales per product. Why is WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY amount DESC) <= 2 the wrong approach?
options: ROW_NUMBER() cannot be used with PARTITION BY
Window functions run after WHERE, so they cannot appear there
It keeps ties that RANK() would drop
PARTITION BY columns must also be listed in a GROUP BY clause
questions.explanation: Window functions run on rows that already passed WHERE and grouping, so they cannot be referenced there. Compute the row number in a CTE or subquery and filter it in the outer query.

questions.text: What does LAG(quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY sale_date) return for each product's earliest sale?
options: The same row's quantity
NULL
The previous product's last quantity
questions.explanation: LAG looks one row back inside the partition; the first row has no predecessor, so the default result is null. Partitions never borrow rows from another product.

questions.text: A report needs each sale's quantity alongside its product's total quantity, keeping one output row per sale. Which expression fits?
options: SUM(quantity) with GROUP BY product_id
SUM(quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id)
SUM(DISTINCT quantity) with GROUP BY sale_id
COUNT(quantity) OVER (ORDER BY product_id)
questions.explanation: An aggregate used as a window function computes across related rows without collapsing them. GROUP BY product_id would return one row per product and lose the individual sales.

questions.text: A recursive CTE walks a category tree downward starting from Computing and returns Computing at depth 0. How do you return only its descendants?
options: Remove the anchor query from the CTE
Change UNION ALL to UNION in the CTE
Filter the final query with WHERE depth > 0
Start the anchor row at depth 1 instead of 0
questions.explanation: The anchor supplies the starting row, and the recursive step builds on it, so removing it returns nothing. Filtering the final result keeps the traversal intact while excluding the starting node.

questions.text: A categories table has parent_id REFERENCES categories(category_id) and CHECK (parent_id <> category_id). Which invalid structure can still be stored?
options: A category whose parent ID does not exist
A category that is its own parent
Two categories that are each other's parent
A root category with a null parent
questions.explanation: The foreign key rejects missing parents and the check rejects a self-loop, but a longer cycle such as A to B to A satisfies both. Traversals should track visited IDs instead of trusting a depth limit.

questions.text: Why can moving a branch be expensive when a tree is stored as materialized paths such as /1/2/5/?
options: Every node's parent ID must be recomputed
Every descendant's stored path string must be rewritten
The whole table must be renumbered with new intervals
A recursive query must run after each insert
questions.explanation: A materialized path stores the traversal result in each row, so moving a subtree changes the prefix of every descendant. Adjacency lists update one parent reference; nested sets renumber intervals.

questions.text:
In this SQLite/PostgreSQL upsert, what does excluded.price_cents refer to?

INSERT INTO catalog (sku, title, price_cents)
VALUES ('BK-10', 'Database Basics, revised', 1600)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET price_cents = excluded.price_cents;
options: The price currently stored in the conflicting row
The price proposed by the insert that conflicted
The price of a previously deleted row
The column's declared default value
questions.explanation: excluded is the pseudo-row holding the values the insert tried to add. The conflict target must match a primary key or unique constraint.

questions.text: Why is SQLite's INSERT OR REPLACE not interchangeable with ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE?
options: It only works on tables without a primary key
It can delete the conflicting row and insert a new one
It silently ignores the new values whenever a conflict occurs
It requires an explicit transaction to run
questions.explanation: Replacing means deleting and reinserting, which can fire delete triggers, affect references and change generated identifiers. An upsert's DO UPDATE modifies the existing row in place.

questions.text: An update intended for product 10 is run as UPDATE products SET price_cents = 2000;. What happens?
options: The statement fails without a WHERE clause
Only the first product row is updated
Every product row gets the new price
Only rows with a null price change
questions.explanation: Without WHERE, UPDATE targets every row in the table. Run risky changes inside a transaction and check the affected-row count before committing.

questions.text: The phone column holds NULL, '' and '12345' in three rows. Which rows does WHERE phone <> '12345' return?
options: The NULL row and the '' row
Only the '' row
Only the NULL row
All three rows
questions.explanation: Comparing null with any value is unknown, not true, so the null row is filtered out. To include missing phones, write phone IS NULL OR phone <> '12345' explicitly.

questions.text: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = 10 AND stock > 0 RETURNING stock; returns no rows. What can the application conclude?
options: The product does not exist in the table
The product exists but is out of stock
No row qualified; the reason needs another check
The update succeeded but RETURNING printed nothing
questions.explanation: An empty RETURNING result means the statement changed nothing. It cannot tell a missing product from one with zero stock; query again if the user needs that distinction.

questions.text: What is the key difference between DELETE FROM products; and DROP TABLE products;?
options: DELETE also removes the table's indexes
DELETE keeps the table; DROP removes it
DROP keeps the rows but removes constraints
They are synonyms that differ only in speed
questions.explanation: DELETE removes rows and leaves an empty table with its columns, constraints and grants. DROP TABLE removes the object, so later queries against it fail.

questions.text: Why is adding a NOT NULL column to a table that already has rows harder than defining it on a new, empty table?
options: NOT NULL columns cannot be added with ALTER TABLE
Existing rows need a default or a backfill
The table's primary key must be dropped first
Existing rows are deleted to satisfy the constraint
questions.explanation: Each existing row would otherwise violate the rule immediately. Choosing a default or backfill is a business decision and usually part of a planned migration.

questions.text: Three customers are combined with three products using CROSS JOIN. How many rows are returned?
options: 0, because there is no join condition
questions.explanation: A cross join returns every pair: 3 × 3 = 9. That is useful when all combinations are intended and a warning sign when a matching condition was accidentally omitted.

questions.text:
Products cost 1500, 2500 and 1800. How many rows does this self-join return?

SELECT a.product_id, b.product_id
FROM products AS a
JOIN products AS b ON a.price_cents < b.price_cents;
questions.explanation: The strict inequality produces one row per cheaper/dearer pair: 1500<1800, 1500<2500 and 1800<2500. It excludes equal-price pairs and a product compared with itself.

questions.text: Why do the notes prefer an explicit ON condition over NATURAL JOIN?
options: NATURAL JOIN always performs a cross join
A new shared column name silently changes the match
NATURAL JOIN ignores the tables' primary keys
NATURAL JOIN is only valid in SQLite databases
questions.explanation: NATURAL JOIN matches on every column with the same name. Adding, say, a status column to both tables would quietly add a matching condition and change results.

questions.text: What does CREATE VIEW order_totals AS SELECT order_id, SUM(...) ... GROUP BY order_id; store?
options: The query definition, evaluated when the view is read
A snapshot of the totals at creation time
A copy of the totals refreshed every hour
An index on order_id that speeds up the totals query
questions.explanation: An ordinary view names a query; later reads see current base data. A materialized view is the variant that stores results and needs a refresh strategy.

questions.text: A SQLite AFTER UPDATE trigger inserts a price-history row, and then the transaction that changed the price rolls back. What remains?
options: The history row, because the trigger ran after the update
Neither the price change nor the history row
The price change, but no history row
Both, because triggers commit on their own
questions.explanation: AFTER means after the row change, not after commit. Trigger writes run inside the same transaction and are rolled back with it.

questions.text: In a row-level UPDATE trigger on products, what do OLD.price_cents and NEW.price_cents refer to?
options: The previous trigger's value and the current trigger's value
The row's price before and after the update
The committed price and the uncommitted price in other sessions
The column's default and its check constraint limit
questions.explanation: OLD holds the row as it was before the statement changed it and NEW holds the proposed row. Comparing them lets a trigger record only real changes or validate a transition.

questions.text: Stock must never be negative. Which mechanism do the notes recommend first?
options: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger that raises an error
A CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint
A stored procedure that all clients must call
An application check before each update
questions.explanation: A declarative constraint directly expresses a single-row rule and applies to every writer. Triggers add less visible behavior and are better reserved for work a constraint cannot express.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, a role has SELECT on public.orders but still cannot query it. Which missing grant is the most likely cause?
options: INSERT on public.orders
USAGE on schema public
REFERENCES on public.orders
TRIGGER on public.orders
questions.explanation: Reading a table needs connect rights on the database, USAGE on its schema and SELECT on the table. Each privilege has a separate purpose.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, you run REVOKE SELECT ON public.orders FROM report_reader; but a user in that role can still read the table. Why might that be?
options: REVOKE only applies after the server restarts
The user gets access through another role, ownership or PUBLIC
REVOKE affects future tables only
Revoked privileges stay active until the next VACUUM finishes
questions.explanation: Revoking removes one grant from one role; it is not an absolute ban. Audit every privilege source, including other role memberships, ownership and grants to PUBLIC.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, how is a function invoked compared with a procedure?
options: Both are invoked only with CALL
A function is used inside SELECT; a procedure is run with CALL
A function runs with EXEC; a procedure is used inside SELECT
Both are invoked only inside triggers
questions.explanation: Functions return a value or set and can appear in queries. Procedures are invoked as statements with CALL and, under specific conditions, may control transactions.

questions.text:
After this transaction commits, what has changed for product 10?

BEGIN;
UPDATE products SET stock = stock + 1 WHERE product_id = 10;
SAVEPOINT optional_change;
UPDATE products SET price_cents = 2000 WHERE product_id = 10;
ROLLBACK TO optional_change;
RELEASE optional_change;
COMMIT;
options: Both the stock and the price
Only the stock
Only the price
Neither the stock nor the price
questions.explanation: Rolling back to a savepoint undoes only work done after it, so the price change is discarded while the earlier stock increment stays and is committed.

questions.text: Work done before a savepoint was kept with ROLLBACK TO, but then the outer transaction runs ROLLBACK. What survives?
options: The work done before the savepoint
The work done after the savepoint
Nothing from the transaction
Whatever was released with RELEASE
questions.explanation: A savepoint is a recovery boundary inside one transaction, not an independently durable commit. Rolling back the outer transaction undoes everything in it.

questions.text: A checkout's stock update succeeds, but the following order insert fails with a duplicate-key error. What should the application do?
options: Commit, since the stock update itself succeeded
Roll back the whole transaction and report or retry
Retry only the failed insert in the same transaction
Ignore the error, as the engine already rolled back
questions.explanation: An error is not automatically a rollback in every engine, and committing would decrease stock without an order. The application decides the boundary and must roll back on any failure.

questions.text: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = 10 AND stock >= 1; affects zero rows inside a checkout transaction. What does that mean for the checkout?
options: The database raised an error and already rolled back
It is a business failure the code must turn into a rollback
Stock was reserved, but no row was reported
The statement must be retried until it affects one row
questions.explanation: A false condition is not a database error. The code must check the affected-row count and refuse the checkout, or it will create an order without reserving stock.

questions.text: An order flow calls a payment API that can take 30 seconds. Where should that call happen?
options: Inside the transaction, so a rollback can undo the payment
Outside the database transaction, keeping the transaction short
Inside a savepoint, so it can be rolled back separately
Inside a trigger on the orders table
questions.explanation: A long transaction can hold locks while it waits, and ROLLBACK cannot undo an external charge or email. Do slow external work outside, and use an outbox for messages that must follow a commit.

questions.text: Why do the notes write an order and an outbox row in the same transaction instead of sending the email directly?
options: So the email is sent before the order commits
So the notification commits or rolls back with it
So ROLLBACK can undo an email already sent
So the worker can never send a message twice
questions.explanation: The outbox makes "send this message" part of the atomic business change. A worker sends after commit, but it can still resend after a crash, so recipients need duplicate tolerance.

questions.text: Which anomaly occurs when a transaction reads a balance that another transaction has written but later rolls back?
options: Dirty read
Non-repeatable read
Phantom read
Write skew
questions.explanation: A dirty read observes uncommitted data that may never become real. Read Committed and stronger levels prevent it.

questions.text: Under Read Committed, a transaction reads a balance twice and sees a different committed value the second time. Which anomaly is this?
options: Uncommitted (dirty) read
Non-repeatable read
Lost update
Phantom read
questions.explanation: Each Read Committed statement can see a newer committed state. Repeatable Read prevents re-reading the same row with a different result; phantoms concern a changing set of matching rows.

questions.text: Two clients each read stock = 10, compute 11 in the application and write it back. The final value is 11. Which fix removes this lost update most simply?
options: Run both reads at Read Uncommitted isolation
Use SET stock = stock + 1 in one UPDATE
Add an index on the stock column first
Read the value twice before writing it
questions.explanation: An atomic relative update lets the database apply both increments to the current row value. The stale calculation came from an unprotected read used for a later write.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL at Repeatable Read, two doctors each count two doctors on call, and each sets only their own row to off call. Both commit. What is this anomaly?
options: Dirty read
Lost update
Write skew
Phantom read
questions.explanation: Each transaction read a consistent snapshot and updated a different row, so neither overwrote the other, yet together they broke "at least one on call". Snapshot isolation permits this.

questions.text: The same doctors schedule runs at PostgreSQL Serializable. What should the application expect?
options: Both transactions commit, leaving nobody on call
One transaction fails with a serialization error to retry
The second SELECT blocks until the first commits
Both transactions are rolled back automatically and silently
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's Serializable Snapshot Isolation detects the dangerous dependency and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001. Do not depend on which session is chosen as the victim.

questions.text: A serializable transaction fails with SQLSTATE 40001. What should the retry do?
options: Re-run only the final UPDATE statement
Restart the whole transaction from its reads
Re-run it at Read Committed to avoid the error
Commit the work that succeeded before the error
questions.explanation: The decision came from reads that are no longer valid. Retrying only the write reuses an obsolete decision; a fresh transaction must read, decide and write again.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL Repeatable Read, transaction A runs SELECT ... WHERE customer_id = 1 twice. Between the two reads, B inserts and commits a matching row. What does A's second read show?
options: The new row, because it is committed
The same rows as the first read
An error, because the snapshot is stale
Only the new row
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL Repeatable Read reads from one transaction snapshot, so ordinary phantoms do not appear. It can still allow write skew.

questions.text: In SQL Server at Repeatable Read, the same sequence runs: a range read, a committed insert of a matching row, then a second range read. What can the second read return?
options: Exactly the same rows, as in PostgreSQL
The newly inserted matching row, a phantom
An error, as the range is locked
Only rows that were updated in between
questions.explanation: SQL Server Repeatable Read holds shared locks on the rows it read, but not on the key range, so new rows can appear. Serializable adds key-range locks to block them.

questions.text: An editor submits UPDATE catalog SET price_cents = 1700, version = version + 1 WHERE product_id = 10 AND version = 1; after another editor already saved version 2. What happens?
options: The price becomes 1700 and the version becomes 3
Zero rows are updated, signalling a conflict
The statement waits until version 1 returns
The database raises a constraint violation
questions.explanation: The version condition no longer matches, so the update affects nothing. This is optimistic concurrency control; the application must check the row count and report the conflict.

questions.text: What must happen before PostgreSQL acknowledges a durable commit under default settings?
options: Every changed data page is written to disk
The commit's WAL records are flushed to durable storage
A checkpoint completes for the database
All replicas confirm that they have applied the change
questions.explanation: Write-ahead logging requires durable log records before acknowledgement; data pages can be written later and replayed from the log after a crash.

questions.text: What is the risk of setting PostgreSQL synchronous_commit = off?
options: The database files can become corrupted after a crash
Recently acknowledged commits can be lost after a crash
Transactions are no longer atomic
Constraints are checked only at checkpoints
questions.explanation: It acknowledges commits before their WAL is flushed, so a crash can lose the latest ones while the database stays consistent. Disabling fsync is far more dangerous and can corrupt the database.

questions.text: The connection drops while a payment transaction is committing, and the client never gets a reply. What is the safe follow-up?
options: Resubmit the payment under a new request ID
Look up the outcome by its stable request ID
Assume the transaction was rolled back
Assume the transaction was committed
questions.explanation: The server may have committed even though the reply was lost. A unique request identifier enforced by a constraint lets the client find the outcome and avoid a duplicate.

questions.text: In two-phase commit, a participant has prepared and then loses contact with the coordinator. What can it do?
options: Commit, because it already voted yes
Roll back once a short timeout expires
Wait in doubt, holding locks, for the decision
Ask another participant to pick the outcome
questions.explanation: A prepared participant cannot guess the global decision without risking inconsistency. In-doubt transactions can hold locks until recovery resolves them, which is a major operational cost.

questions.text: How do two-phase commit (2PC) and two-phase locking (2PL) relate?
options: 2PL is the commit step inside 2PC
2PC agrees on commit; 2PL controls access
They are two names for one protocol
2PC replaces 2PL on single-node databases
questions.explanation: 2PC makes several participants agree to commit or abort. 2PL is a locking discipline for serializable schedules. The similar names do not make them the same mechanism.

questions.text: Under traditional shared/exclusive locking, which request on the same row is granted immediately?
options: A shared lock while another shared lock is held
An exclusive lock while a shared lock is held
A shared lock while an exclusive lock is held
An exclusive lock while an exclusive lock is held
questions.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with each other, so readers can share. Any combination involving an exclusive lock on the same resource conflicts.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, session A has updated a row but not committed. Session B runs an ordinary SELECT of that row at Read Committed. What happens?
options: B blocks until A commits or rolls back
B reads the last committed version at once
B sees A's uncommitted change immediately
B fails with a lock-timeout error
questions.explanation: MVCC lets ordinary reads use a committed snapshot instead of taking blocking shared row locks. A locking read such as FOR SHARE or FOR UPDATE would wait.

questions.text: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT change when the row is already locked?
options: It makes the two locks compatible
It raises an error instead of waiting
It skips the locked row and returns others
It reads the row without any lock
questions.explanation: NOWAIT changes only the waiting behaviour: fail immediately rather than block. It does not make incompatible locks compatible; skipping rows is what SKIP LOCKED does.

questions.text:
Several workers claim jobs with this query while job 100 is locked by another worker. What does a worker get?

SELECT job_id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY job_id
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;
options: It waits for the lock on job 100 to be released
The next unlocked pending job, such as 101
An error because job 100 is locked
Job 100, read without a lock
questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED ignores rows other transactions have locked, which suits queues. It deliberately gives an inconsistent view, so it is not for general transactional reads.

questions.text: T1 locks account A then requests B, while T2 locks B then requests A. Which design change prevents this deadlock?
options: Raising the lock timeout for both transactions
Always locking accounts in the same order, such as by ID
Using NOLOCK hints on the updates
Retrying each failed statement until it eventually succeeds
questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits. Acquiring locks in a consistent global order makes the cycle impossible; timeouts and retries only react after it happens.

questions.text: What does PostgreSQL's deadlock_timeout setting (default 1 second) control?
options: The maximum runtime allowed for any query
How long a transaction may hold any lock
How long a lock wait lasts before deadlock checks
How long a deadlock victim waits before it is retried
questions.explanation: Deadlock detection has a cost, so PostgreSQL runs it only after a lock wait lasts this long. It is not a general query or lock timeout.

questions.text: PostgreSQL aborts a transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01. What happened?
options: A serialization failure with no lock cycle
A deadlock was detected; it was the victim
A lock-wait timeout expired for a statement
A unique constraint was violated on insert
questions.explanation: 40P01 is deadlock_detected; 40001 is a serialization failure, which needs no wait cycle. Both are retriable by rerunning the whole transaction.

questions.text: What rule defines two-phase locking?
options: Locks are acquired in two batches of equal size
Once a transaction releases any lock, it acquires no new locks
Every lock is held for exactly two statements
Shared locks are always taken first, then exclusive locks
questions.explanation: A growing phase that only acquires is followed by a shrinking phase that only releases. This guarantees conflict serializability but not freedom from deadlock.

questions.text: What does strict 2PL add to basic two-phase locking?
options: All locks are acquired before the transaction starts
Exclusive locks are held until commit or abort
Shared locks are never released
Deadlocks become impossible
questions.explanation: Holding write locks to the end stops other transactions reading uncommitted data, avoiding cascading aborts. Conservative 2PL, not strict 2PL, pre-acquires all locks.

questions.text: T1 waits for a row lock held by T2, and T2 is busy with a long update that waits on nothing T1 holds. What is this situation?
options: A deadlock that the database must break
Blocking that ends when T2 commits or rolls back
A livelock between the two transactions
A serialization failure that is awaiting a retry
questions.explanation: Blocking is a one-way wait that resolves when the holder finishes. A deadlock needs a cycle, such as T2 also waiting for T1, so that no transaction can ever proceed.

questions.text: Why can SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on existing booking rows fail to prevent a double booking?
options: FOR UPDATE only locks rows for reading
It cannot lock a row that does not exist yet
It releases its locks after each statement
It is ignored at Read Committed
questions.explanation: Row locks protect existing rows, not the absence of a matching row. Use a constraint, a range or predicate mechanism, Serializable, or lock a row that represents the resource itself.

questions.text: What does SQL Server's WITH (NOLOCK) hint actually do?
options: Uses finer-grained row locks for the query
Reads with roughly Read Uncommitted semantics
Releases other transactions' locks on the table
Makes the query fully serializable
questions.explanation: NOLOCK is an isolation choice, not a lock-size tuning switch. It can return dirty, missing or duplicated rows.

questions.text: An application runs BEGIN on one pooled connection and its next UPDATE on a different connection. What is true?
options: Both statements share the same transaction
The UPDATE is not part of the first connection's transaction
The pool merges the two connections into one session automatically
The UPDATE waits until the first connection commits
questions.explanation: Transaction state belongs to a connection. Returning an unfinished transaction to the pool can also surprise the next borrower.
